text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Swedish unemployment will fall this autumn and the downward trend will strengthen next year, a forecast by the Labour Market Board (Ams) shows. However, unemployment will still rise to a total of 8.4 percent in 1997 from 8.1 percent last year, Ams forecast.
- Real estate group Hufvudstaden bid for rival Fabege, aiming to create a real estate group with a market capitalisation of 10 billion crowns.
- Metals and mining group Trelleborg declines comment on a one year strike at its Boliden unit's plant in Copperhill, Tennessee, despite the conflict escalating.
- Nine out of 10 Swedish teachers over 45 years of age think their job is so tough that they doubt being able to stay on until retirement at 65.

- The Swedish central bank's position has become stronger after a five-party agreement on Tuesday. The Riksbank will have new management and it will keep responsibility for running monetary policy while the government will make decisions about what exchange rate system the country should have.

- State-owned power company Vattenfall's chairman Karl-Erik Sahlberg stepped down on Tuesday, saying that the company's position will be impossible when it should both compete on the market and be "a resource" in the restructuring work after the phase out of listed Sydkraft's nuclear power plant Barseback. Parliament has ruled to phase out Barseback, starting with the first of the two reactors in 1998.

- Two large Swedish companies have been sold to foreign owners. Ellos, the Swedish mail order company was sold to the French firm La Redoute for between two and three billion crowns by Swedish investment company Industri Kapital which paid 780 million crowns for its share in Ellos ony two years ago. Finnish power group Imatran Voima Oy (IVO) became the largest owner in Gullspang in a 2.7 billion crown deal as Swedish utility companies Vattenfall and Graninge sold their stakes.

- The man behind Astra's blockbusting anti-ulcer Losec drug, Ivan Ostholm, says he has a new drug underway for a disease afflicting the elderly. Losec now accounts for 45 percent of Astra's sales. Ostholm says the new project has huge potential and investors will have the chance to buy shares in the project in the summer.
- Finance Minister Erik Asbrink says he does not believe in the U.S. model against unemployment which includes low wages and high movement within the labour market.

- Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom won a small victory -- he does not have to concern himself with unemployment. He only has to keep taking care of inflation, following a five-party agreement announced by the Finance Ministry on Tuesday.
